Modern.tagline: The case that traveled the world.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Named for the Wardian case — the sealed glass terrarium invented by Nathaniel Bagshaw Ward in 1829, which made it possible to transport live plants across oceans without losing them to salt spray. The Wardian case enabled the global houseplant trade, including the Victorian tea industry. We name the shop after the object that made indoor plants a global category. The Wardian case is a public-domain object, not a trademark.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern plant shops are crowded with Instagram-first retailers selling the same fiddle-leaf figs and monsteras. There is room for a modern plant brand whose identity is rooted in the actual history of how indoor plants traveled — and whose product range includes glass terrariums and rare imports.
Modern.competitorLandscape: The Sill (thesill.com) holds the modern-DTC slot. Pistils Nursery (pistilsnursery.com) is the considered-modern peer. Greenery Unlimited (greeneryunlimited.co) sets the design-led precedent. We sit closer to Pistils, sharper on the Wardian-case anchor.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern plant shop built around the history of the portable greenhouse.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Owns thirty houseplants. Reads House Plant Hobbyist. Knows the difference between epiphyte and hemiepiphyte.

dos: Name the species, the origin, the care
Print the genus and species on the tag
Speak in the language of the grower

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark with a Wardian-case hallmark. Wardian Co. set in a tight modern grotesk, paired with a small line-drawing of a Wardian case as the brand's hallmark. The case alone is the favicon.

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and signage
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for genus, species, and care data
typography.rationale: The mono carries the botanical specification. The regular carries the brand.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Named for Sir Joseph Banks, the botanist on Cook's first Endeavour voyage (1768–1771), whose Pacific specimen collections seeded the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew and helped found the global botanical archive. Banks is a historical figure long out of estate (died 1820); his name is in the public domain and has been used by multiple natural-history institutions for centuries. We name the shop after the botanist whose specimens defined the field.
Luxury.industrySummary: Luxury plant retail is a small but durable segment — rare aroids, variegated monsteras, and conservatory-grade specimens. There is room for a luxury plant brand with an explorer-archive aesthetic, modeled on the 18th-century botanist's archive rather than the modern hipster plant shop.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Pistils Nursery (pistilsnursery.com) holds the considered-luxury slot. Steve's Leaves (stevesleaves.com) is the rare-specimen peer. Logee's Greenhouses (logees.com) sets the heritage-specimen precedent. We sit above all three in retail framing.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A luxury rare-plants house with an 18th-century explorer-archive identity.

targetAudience.primary: 40 to 65. Owns a heated conservatory or a south-facing room. Buys a single specimen for $400 and waits a year for it.

dos: Name the explorer, the voyage, the herbarium
Print the botanical Latin on every tag
Issue a hand-bound care guide with every specimen

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark with a hand-drawn specimen hallmark. Banks Botanical set in a high-contrast classical serif, paired with a single hand-illustrated leaf specimen as the mark, foiled in copper on every tag.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and signage
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for botanical Latin and care data
typography.rationale: Canela carries the archive stance. The mono carries the botanical specification.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Named for foliage — the trade term for non-flowering ornamental leaves, the category that drives most houseplant retail. A one-word minimal brand whose entire range is green-leaf plants. Foliage is a generic trade term, not a trademark.
Minimal.industrySummary: Minimal plant shops can compete by claiming a single category as their entire range. A one-word brand named after the foliage category itself — green leaves only, no flowering plants — has no peer.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: The Sill (thesill.com) holds the modern-DTC slot. Greenery NYC (greenerynyc.com) is the considered-minimal peer. Leon & George (leonandgeorge.com) sets the design-minimal precedent. We sit below all three on visual noise.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A minimal plant shop selling only foliage plants.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 40. Lives in a one-bedroom. Owns five plants. Wants more, but not flowering ones.
behaviors: Repots in a single pot color

dos: Say nothing the care card doesn't say

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark. FOLIAGE set in a tight modern grotesk, with a single leaf silhouette as the hallmark. The leaf alone is the favicon.

typography.secondary: Söhne Mono for genus, species, and care data
typography.rationale: One typeface family. The mono carries the care data, the regular carries the brand.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Named for the 19th-century botanical-supply trade pioneered by James Veitch & Sons and other Victorian nursery firms, which supplied estate gardens, conservatories, and the early commercial plant trade. As a corporate name, Botanical Supply Co. positions the brand as a B2B-friendly umbrella for wholesale, interior plantscaping, and multi-location retail.
Corporate.industrySummary: The B2B side of the plant industry — interior plantscaping for offices, hospitality, and retail — is fragmented and dominated by regional installers. There is room for a corporate-feeling umbrella that serves wholesale, plantscape installation, and retail garden centers under one identity.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Ambius (ambius.com) holds the global plantscape slot. Plantscape Inc. (plantscape.com) is the regional installer peer. Costa Farms (costafarms.com) sets the wholesale-grower precedent. We sit between Ambius and Costa Farms.
Corporate.positioningStatement: A corporate-feeling umbrella for plant wholesale, plantscape installation, and retail.

targetAudience.primary: Hospitality buyers, office facilities managers, retail garden center procurement. Buys by the truckload.

dos: Quote lead times and pallet quantities

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a hallmark. Botanical Supply Co. set in a clean American sans-serif, paired with a simple shield containing a stylized leaf-and-pot silhouette.

typography.primary: Aktiv Grotesk for the wordmark and headers
typography.secondary: Aktiv Grotesk for body and price lists
typography.rationale: One typeface family. Reads professional on a purchase order and clean on a shipping crate.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Named for Daniel Solander — Banks's botanist on the Endeavour — and for the 'Solander box,' the archival book-box he invented for storing pressed plant specimens. The Solander box remains the standard archival container in herbaria and museum print rooms today. The shop's monthly subscription delivers a curated specimen in a Solander-style archival case. Solander is a historical figure (died 1782); the term Solander box is in general usage in archival science.
Creative.industrySummary: Plant subscription boxes are crowded with monthly-flower and monthly-houseplant services. There is creative room for a curated specimen subscription whose presentation references the 18th-century botanical archive — a single rare plant per month, delivered in an archival case with a hand-printed care guide.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Bloomscape (bloomscape.com) holds the DTC-houseplant slot. Léon & George (leonandgeorge.com) is the considered-subscription peer. Hortology (hortology.co.uk) sets the rare-specimen precedent. We sit alongside Hortology, sharper on the archival-case framing.
Creative.positioningStatement: A creative monthly subscription delivering one curated plant specimen in an archival case.
